  and a stick - brings up bones, flint, potsherds, stone tools and grain, and one find in four is a piece of the
  ruin's Pioneer tablet. A piece shows some of the figure's digits; pieces of one tablet, one in each hand, join,
  and when every digit shows they are the whole tablet. A piece from another ruin does not fit.
- **An archive in war.** The Covenant forbids burning an archive. In a war window, a warrior of the other side
  who reaches a town's Society may use its register with paper: each sheet becomes a hurried copy of the next
  work the archive holds, one every five seconds. The originals stay; the chronicle notes it.
- **Wounds that show.** An open wound on a body dirty enough for a healer to remark on is drawn grimy over the
  player, an infected one festering yellow, for everybody near to see. The texture is a placeholder.

### The atlas: sickness, named rivers and ridges, orders, meetings, blank spots and north
- **Cases of illness on the map.** Every case that shows is noted where it showed. Your own page marks where
  you fell ill in the last month; a citizen's town page marks every citizen's, one mark per spot with the
  number of cases, so a cluster round one well can be seen. A disease is named on the map only if you know it;
  otherwise the mark just says people fell ill.
- **Rivers and ridges have names.** Wading a river puts its reach on your map; reading the water beside it
  with an instrument (a plane table points there) puts it on at that reading's accuracy. A reach on your map at
  sketch or better can be named in a Society's register, like a ridge. A theodolite on a ridge now also marks
  its summit on your map. Named rivers and ridges are lettered on every map that shows them, and listed in the
  atlas margin.
- **Survey orders.** Pin a drawn sheet to the town board as the sample of an order, and the order asks for a
  sheet of the same kind, of the same ground, drawn since it went up - "a new soil map of the valley, I pay".
  Only such a sheet answers it; a copy of an old one does not.
- **Swapping sketches.** Two travellers each holding a field map or an expedition plan: one uses theirs on
  the other, and each gets a copy of the other's, drawn on a blank sheet from their own pack. Office sheets are
  sold, not swapped.
- **The world's blank spots.** In a library (a building that keeps books) the atlas has a fourth tab: every
  record on the server merged into a single shade - where somebody has been, and where nobody has. Not what is
  there.
- **North.** With a compass (vanilla, the magnetic compass or the surveying compass) about you, atlas pages lie
  north-up. Without one, the top of the page is the way you faced when you opened it; the compass rose in the
  corner says where north went, and the arrows leaf the way they point on the screen.
- **The surveying compass corrects for declination.** Crouch and use it to take a bearing for the map: a
  surveyed bearing once you can predict the declination (a few noon sightings, or a work on it), a sketch -
  no better than the plain compass - until then.

### The levy, debts and the tax form
- **A levy on every citizen.** A town's head or treasurer decrees so many coins of one metal a week from every
  citizen - `/polity decree levy <coins> <metal>`, or the new tax form on the town page. Like the market tax it
  waits a day, a council town votes on it first, and nought lifts it. Nothing is taken from anybody's pack:
  the levy is charged on its weekly day and paid at the hall with **Pay the levy**, in coins of that metal of
  any stamp, the town's own first - all of it, or as much as one carries.
- **Debts and debtors.** What is still unpaid when the next levy falls is a debt. The town page lists its
  debtors for anybody to read, and a debtor is told at login. No ban and no fine; a debt outlives the charter
  and is not forgiven by lifting the levy. The chronicle notes a levy coming into force and being lifted.
- **The tax form.** The town page has a **Taxes** button for the head and the treasurer: the market tax and
  the levy, each a number and a button, checked again by the server. The treasurer may now decree the market
  tax as well; a stipend is still the head's. Operators read and force the levy with `/polity levy <town>`
  and `/polity levy fall <town>`. See `docs/economy/levy.md`.

- **The library catalogue finds Russian titles.** A search matched only a book's English title and author, so
  a search typed in Russian found nothing although the shelves read in Russian. The catalogue now matches a
  title and author as either language reads them, and takes "е" for "ё".
- **Nobody is an empty name.** Somebody the server had never seen - an offline test name - was written into
  the chronicle and onto papers as an empty string. A record now keeps the chosen name, or "Stranger (mark)"
  for somebody met but unnamed, or the account name for somebody never met, and a plain stranger at worst;

- **`/polity caravan carriages` says what is true.** A taken carriage showed "0 goods" and a finished one
  "pays 0". A carriage on the road now counts the goods under seal in its cart, and a finished one says where

### Living landscape: wildfires and regrowth
- **Wildfires.** Lightning striking ground in drought can start a forest fire. How dry the soil is decides
  whether it catches and how far it may run; the front crosses about a block every five seconds, rain slows it,
  and players nearby smell the smoke. It burns only what grows - leaves, undergrowth, grass, whole Dynamic
  Trees - and stops at the first thing that was built. Operators can start and put out fires with
  `/forestry wildfire start|stop|list`.
- **Burns.** A tree leaves a **charred trunk** that gives charcoal and falls a block at a time over months;
  grass and forest litter burn down to bare soil, patched with **ash** that keeps the grass out until wind or
  rain takes it. The ecosystem loses the nitrogen to smoke and keeps phosphorus and potash as ash, and the
  soil sweetens; the atlas sees the fire.
- **Regrowth in order.** Pines, aspens, birches, sequoias and acacias come back from their own fire, a sapling
  by the trunk a few days on. Elsewhere pioneers - birch, aspen, pine, acacia, willow, kapok, Douglas fir -
  seed into open light first, and shade-tolerant maple, spruce, white cedar, hickory, oak, chestnut and
  sycamore come up beneath them later. `/forestry wildfire list` shows each burn's stage.

### Rivers with character, and geology by seed
- **Fords.** Where a river is narrow enough to shoal, a bar of gravel and stones of the local rock crosses it
  with one block of water over it: the way across on foot, and where the salmon pack in the run: while a run is on,
  the catch on the shallows - fords and rapids - is half as large again.
- **Rapids.** On narrow rivers, a reach where the bed comes up in broken rock and boulders stand out of the
  current; a boat does not get through and is carried round.
- **Floodplains.** Low ground along a wide river is laid in fluvisol, the alluvial soil, which the ecosystem
  reads as silt: it holds water and nutrients better than the loams round it. Now and then an **oxbow** - a
  crescent of still water where the river used to bend - lies on the plain.
- **The spring flood** reaches the plain: while the river is in flood the world model is told (the atlas can
  draw it), and while it falls it leaves silt - nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium and humus back into the
  fields of the plain. No water is moved; nobody loses a house to it. New chunks only.
- **Geology by seed.** `tools/worldgen_seed.py` writes a datapack from a world's seed before it is first
  started: ores move between rocks of the same family, and each ore lies only in a few districts, one near
  spawn. `/worldgen districts`, `/worldgen ores` and `/worldgen rivers` show an operator what is where. See
  `SERVER_SETUP.md`.
- **Rivers are water.** TerraFirmaCraft's river water is its own fluid, outside the vanilla water tag, so the
  spear, the hand line and the casting net found nothing in a river, a drink from one was not counted, and the
  microscope would not take a sample from one. They all use `#realism:open_water` now: the vanilla tag and the
  river.
- **Traps and lines go in rivers.** The fish trap and the longline could only be placed in plain water, so
  never in a river; a crock would not take river water from a jug; and a player under a river was not
  diving, so a cold river never chilled. All three read `#realism:open_water` now; a crock keeps what it
  takes as plain water, which is what recipes ask for.
- **Seen in the assembled client, fixed.** On a 320x240 screen in Russian the atlas's "Листы (0)" tab and
  the town page's "Договоры" were clipped - tabs now take the width their labels need; the tax form's
  "Назначить налог, %" button was cut and its note ran off under the Back button - the button is sized
  to its label and a note that does not fit ends in an ellipsis with the whole of it as a tooltip. The
  name screen's example mark read as typed text; field hints are grey now. One door read as two ways
  out in a building's survey. A book used in the hand did nothing a new player could make sense of; it
  now says it is read at a Reading Desk, and so does its tooltip. Distant Horizons asked every player to
  update it on the first start; its updater is off.
- **A bed makes a citizen at once.** Setting a bed in a house in town made its sleeper a resident only at the
  next sweep, twenty minutes later; the town reads its houses again the moment a bed is set. Russian coin
  amounts read "2 мон." instead of the ungrammatical "2 монет", and the town page's bottom buttons are as wide
  as their labels ("Сложить гражданство" was cut).
- **A catalogue search takes a Russian word in any form.** "зима" finds "Как пережить первую зиму" and
  "воды" finds "Вода, и можно ли ей верить": a Russian word loses its last vowels before it is looked for,
  and a search of several words finds the books that have all of them. Russian messages that put a
  person's name after a preposition ("Вы с Незнакомец", "Письмо от Незнакомец") are worded so the name

- **Where you stand is the building you are in.** An open market square measures a wide stretch of ground,
  and a library built on that ground answered its catalogue search as the square - no volumes, nothing found.
  The tightest building round a player is now the one meant. A building in a town with no treasury yet read
  "outside any town, nobody pays it"; it now says it is in the town and that nobody pays it yet.
- **Fresh water has fresh fish.** A trap in a river came up with oysters, red coral and cod: the catch

- **Spring starts in March.** How far through its season the TFC calendar is came out wrong by a month: March

### The living atlas, and science paid for
- **The atlas opens at your own survey.** Everybody is handed one atlas on their first day. Opened, it is a
  spread: a page of the map drawn from your own record - pencil where you walked, ink where you measured -
  and a margin with the legend. Three scales (1, 2 and 4 km to the page); the arrows, the arrow keys and the
  wheel leaf and zoom it. A citizen has a second tab, **the town's survey**: every citizen's record merged,
  with the names of those who drew most of the page. The bound sheets are the third tab, as before.
  Crouching with a blank sheet in the other hand takes the page you stand on down onto paper, with no table.
- **Lost only in the blank.** By your town's hall or your bed you know exactly where you are. On ground you
  know - a road, a signpost in sight, country your own survey had before today - the error is small and
  walking does not grow it. Anywhere else, dead reckoning drifts as it always did.
- **Roads measure themselves.** Walking a road books the plot under your feet a step better than walking
  alone - only that plot, so a road becomes a fine line on the map and the fields beside it stay a sketch.
- **Signposts.** A sign and two sticks. What you letter on it ("Bend, 2 km") goes onto every map in the
  world, and anybody who can see it knows roughly where they are.
- **Landmarks by themselves.** A town's hall seen from the road and a ford waded go onto your map as a sketch.
- **Icons and winter.** Every point on a map is a drawn icon that reads at any scale; notes in the margin sit
  on a paper disc, signposts and towns in a square frame. A living page lays snow on the land when it is
  freezing where you stand.
- **Stipends and printing licences.** A town head decrees, like the market tax, a stipend in coins for every
  work the town's Society accepts (`/polity decree stipend <coins> <metal>`) and a fee for another town's
  press to print a work under the town's privilege (`/polity decree licence <coins> <metal>`). The author
  collects the stipend at the register; a press in another town pays the fee from its treasury for every
  run. A treasury that is short says so in its book and the stipend stays owed.


### Late science: expeditions, instruments of the third kind, printing
- **Expeditions.** A Society's register fits out an expedition to a target written as x and z, for thirty
  days; the charter puts others on it and, brought back, is the report. A **theodolite** reads how high a place
  stands over the sea; high in the mountains the line is about the ridge - the same 512-block square for
  anyone who climbs there - and a ridge can be named before a Society. A member who dies out in the field
  leaves a **cairn** with copies of their notebooks; a party of another expedition that finds it is written
  into the chronicle.
- **Instruments of the third kind.** A **chronometer** set at home tells longitude at noon anywhere else. An
  **assay furnace** reads an ore to a hundredth. A **microscope** in a laboratory shows living things in a
  vial of water: whoever sees them drops miasma and knows the waterborne fevers, and the first time goes into
  the chronicle.
- **Standards.** An academy - a Society of the higher grade - makes the world's standard weight, thermometer
  and measure, once each. Calibrating against one quarters what calibration leaves unknown. Carried out of its
  keeper's town by a stranger, a standard is stolen, and the keeper's Society declares it - a crime a war can
  be declared on.
- **Ciphers.** A cipher key puts a notebook beyond anybody without it; a copy stays in cipher. A counting board
  breaks a notebook of forty lines for a reader of statistics, with eight sheets of paper.
- **Printing.** The printing press prints treatises and tables ten at a time, with no copyist's slips; for a
  year after a work is accepted, only the presses of the accepting town may print it. The first print in the
  world goes into the chronicle.
- **Societies together.** Societies recognise each other's registers; later names for the same thing show as
  synonyms; a work becomes a law only with another author or a recognised second Society. A rung above a
  series ages back to it ninety days after the player's last line on the law, and what they know of it widens.
- **Trophies and tablets.** Whoever kills an enemy in war carries off copies of their notebooks. Barrows and
  cellars of the Pioneers hold **tablets**: laws as the world was when it was young, cut by a hand that slipped.
- **Old wounds.** A break left without a splint knits crooked - a twentieth off the pace for each, three at
  most - and an infected wound that heals leaves a scar; both outlive a death. In an **anatomical theatre** a
  healer who has set ten bones breaks a crooked one and sets it true.


### The living world
- **Chapters.** The chronicle's years begin because of what happened: the Years of Boundaries when towns meet,
  of Bells when the first relic stands on a pedestal, of Leagues with the first league or vassal; each is
  foretold three days ahead. War by the Covenant waits for the Years of Bells. Operators may declare the
  Troubles (`/polity epoch`).
- **Disasters** come a day after their omen, in the dry words of an observer: crop failure, a harsh winter,
  murrain, an epidemic that spreads between people standing close and is stopped by a quarantine house. Now
  and then the world brings one by itself; operators start them with `/polity disaster`.
- **Ruins.** A town none of whose people came for a month is a ruin: new towns may be founded over it, its
  relic is laid to rest, and anyone without a charter may take it up - with its debts and feuds
  (`/polity town claim`).
- **Newcomers** take a charter in any town by themselves for their first week (`/polity settle`) and are out
  of reach of blows for three days.
- **Nicknames and titles.** The first oak a person fells, the first relic they carry home, their first broken
  bone give them a nickname the chronicle calls them by; three victories as general or ten patients earn a
  title. `/polity chronicle me` is one's own chronicle.
- The world's laws drift slowly with its age: a series measured a year ago predicts worse than a fresh one.

### Science: the ladder of knowledge, the Society, instruments that drift
- Every law of the world - a herb's strength, an ore's metal, a steel's quench, a calx's gain, the compass
  declination - stands on a **rung** for each player: hearsay, practice, observation, series, hypothesis,
  test, work, priority, law. The rung is read off the player's notebooks, hypotheses, entries and reading,
  never stored as points; `/almanac laws` lists them. A herb works as well as its healer knows it: by luck on
  hearsay, steadily from practice up.
- **Hypotheses** on paper: paper at the field desk opens a page of claims the carried notebooks support - a
  law lies between two numbers, two plots give differently, a received theory is wrong - to be named and
  written on a sheet. Held at the desk, the sheet is put to the lines written since, a full batch at a time:
  nothing is said until the batch is in, and one line outside its own error refutes it.
- **Plots**: a stake with a letter (a dye moves it on) turns the crops harvested beside it into that plot's
  lines in the notebook. The page compares two plots; a reader with a little statistics is told whether they
  differ.
- **Instruments of the second kind**: a thermometer, a steelyard with its two-kilogram weight, a quadrant, a
  surveying compass and a rain gauge. Each reads off by its own zero and stretch until it is put to points
  whose value is known by definition - ice and a boiling pot, an empty hook and the weight, the horizon and
  the plumb line, an empty gauge and a bucket - and wanders a little every season after. The pyrometer is
  calibrated the same way, on a boiling pot and a lava cauldron.
- **The quench is a law of the world**: TFC Heat Treatment's best band sits where this world puts it for each
  metal, up to sixty degrees from the numbers JEI shows. A smith carrying a pyrometer writes down where a
  best quench came from.
- **The Society**: a building of two storeys with archive cabinets, a desk, seats and a **Society register**.
  Its register takes names for identified species, measured ores and known diseases, and works on laws and
  refutations borne out on paper; priority goes to the moment of entry. Members with theory in the subject
  accept or refuse entries; a secretary takes whatever waits three days, and refuses one in four. The
  earliest accepted name stands for everybody - in the tooltip, at the desk, in the notebook, at the healer's
  diagnosis - and goes into the chronicle. A work accepted by a second hand or a second Society becomes a law.
- **Paper**: an accepted work comes back as a **treatise**. Reading one lifts the reader to its rung, but no
  higher than their theory in the subject lets them follow. Crouching with a treatise in a building that
  copies writes it onto paper, or its figures into a **table**; a copyist with little schooling gets one
  figure in twenty wrong, and only the Society's original, held against the register, shows which copy is
  right. A table of quench temperatures with a slipped figure sends a blade into the water too hot.
- **False paradigms**: every player starts out believing in miasma, phlogiston and spontaneous generation,
  and they cost a little - dressings, clean rooms, assays and crocks all go worse. A fever from water with no
  filth near it, a calx heavier than its metal on a calibrated steelyard, and a crock that stayed clean a week
  under its stone are written down as anomalies; three of them let the theory be refuted on paper.

### Medicine as knowledge
- A healer's **casebook** carries the cases they examine in a clinic. Read in a clinic it teaches its cases
  to someone else; crouched over with another where books are copied, the two are bound into one.
- A treatise on a disease teaches its reader to recognise it; without the cases or the treatise a healer
  still sees only the signs.
- Grandmother's remedies: a **bloodletting lancet** eases a fever and leaves the patient weak and the illness
  faster; a **hot compress** comforts a wound and hastens its festering.
- **Dirt** builds up on a body in dung, at butchering and in fights, gets into wounds, and comes off in water,
  in rain, and in half a minute in a **bathhouse** (which clears the itch as well). A healer's dirty hands
  dirty the wounds they dress; crouching in water washes them.
- **Boiled bandages** - bandages used on a boiling pot - are clean for a day; a dressing in a hospital's clean
  room leaves a tenth of the dirt. A **latrine** fouls the water in its ground, five times over with typhoid
  about, and a **quarantine house** keeps the sick from passing it on through their beds.

### War II and politics
- **Posts and roles.** Officers and a general on the muster roll; before a war's first window its head or
  general hands out roles - general, standard-bearer, guard, messenger, medic, sapper, scout - each with a sash
  in its colour and what it does in a window. Small sides merge roles; mercenaries are hired for coin; the
  larger side fights with as many as the smaller. See `WAR.md`.
- **Spoils.** A declaration names a contribution, weekly tribute, land at the boundary, or a month's
  vassalage. A vassal pays, sends half its roll to its suzerain's wars, and answers to a governor who may veto
  its decrees; its citizens may conspire in secret and rise in one window to win their relic home.
- **Alliances, peace, boundaries, leagues.** New treaties on the Treaties tab: an alliance lets a town join
  its ally's war, a peace forbids war between two, a boundary sets where two neighbours' border runs. Three
  towns allied each to each may found a league (`/polity league`).
- **Reputation** now moves with alliances and peaces kept or broken, ransoms, war crimes, exiles and vassals;
  at -50 a town is an outlaw, open to war without a grievance.
- **Government.** A town is a chiefdom (a regent stands in for a head away a week), a council (war, treaties
  and taxes go to a day's vote) or a republic (the head is elected every two weeks). A referendum of two thirds
  changes it; a petition of more than half deposes the head (`/polity government`, `vote`, `referendum`,
  `coup`).

### The foreign trader
- Once a season a foreign trader comes to a town with a market square and an inn, and walks from the road
  to the square. He sells only what is not had near the town - tropical dye plants, northern ones, Firmalife
  spices, polished marble and quartzite - for silver coin of any stamp, cheaper for a town of good name, and
  moves on after two days. Killing him is a robbery the chronicle and the war remember, and he does not come
  back for a year.
- A robbery somebody saw, of the trader or of a caravan, now costs the robber's town reputation.

### Caravans
- Goods travel between towns in a cart or on a pack animal. A **waybill** from the hall's board (a sheet of
  paper) seals a loaded TFC Astikor cart, or a donkey or mule with a chest, at its town; the caravan counts
  its road and its share of it by road, and arrives inside the other town near its hall or market. A journey
  of 200 blocks or more goes into the chronicle.
- **Carriages** on the board's new page: goods and a reward from your two hands, a deadline and a deposit in
  the reward's kind. A carrier puts down the deposit and the goods load into their cart, sealed, in one step;
  handed over at the other hall, the goods wait there for the shipper and the carrier is paid the reward and
  the deposit back. Robbed, lost, left or late, the shipper gets both. A treasury can send one.
- **Robbery** outside every town - opening the load, breaking the cart, killing the animal, leading it away -
  ends the caravan, is written in the chronicle (the robber named only with a witness) and is reported as a
  crime the war can take as a grievance. Inside any town, and anywhere from a minute after its carrier leaves
  the game, nobody else may touch a caravan, and its deadlines stand still while the carrier is away.
- An animal pulling a cart is quicker on a road, as a ridden one already was.

### Treaties, loans and reputation
- Towns sign treaties. A head offers one on the new **Treaties** tab of the town page; the other town's
  head signs or declines it at their own hall, and each archive keeps its copy. An offer lapses after a
  week unanswered.
- A **trade treaty** lowers the market tax for the other town's citizens - each side sets its own rate -
  for 14, 28 or 56 days. Kept to its end, both towns gain reputation; the town that breaks it early loses
  some.
- A **loan** moves coin or goods from one treasury to another, at 0-50 % for 1-56 days. On its day the
  borrower's treasury pays back what it holds: all of it keeps the loan, less breaks it, and the rest can
  be paid back later. The lender can forgive what is left.
- Every town has a **reputation** from -100 to 100 with the reasons it moved, on the town page, the
  Treaties tab and `/polity town list`. Treaty lines are written into both towns' chronicles.

### The market
- A town can hold a market. A **market square** is a new building: 48 m² of ground, open or in a hall,
  with four **market stalls** (cloth over lumber over two sticks) on it; a covered market - a hall of two
  storeys - shows eight lots on every stall instead of four. Upkeep: two lumber a week.
- A seller puts goods up at a stall with both hands - the goods in one, one of the price in the other -
  and goes about their day; a buyer pays and takes them while the seller is away. The goods and the money
  are kept by the town's market book, not by the block: breaking a stall hands every lot back to its
  seller, now or the next time they come. A coin's stamp is part of its price.
- The head decrees a **market tax** of up to 25 % (`/polity decree tax <percent>`), in force a day after it
  is issued. Every sale gives the treasury its share, in the price's own items, with a line in the ledger;
  what a sale owes below one item is carried to the lot's next sale. The chronicle notes the tax.
- Every sale goes into the town's **price history**, one point a day and price, on the Prices page of any
  stall. Operators can look at a market and trade on it from the console (`/polity market`).

### War by the Covenant
- New module `realism-war`. A town joins the Covenant by setting its relic - a bell, an ark, an idol, a banner
  or a millstone - on a pedestal in its hall, and chooses what it does while it stands at home: cheaper upkeep,
  faster work orders or better fields. Only towns in the Covenant make war, and only on each other.
- A war needs a grievance the world recorded (a citizen killed, a building damaged, goods taken, an armed party
  in the border, a breach of the Covenant). The head declares it with a demand of up to a quarter of the other
  treasury; the defender accepts, or refuses and chooses the hour of three two-hour windows on three evenings.
  Outside the windows nobody fights and no relic can be lifted.
- In a window, the side that carries the other's relic home and holds it on a pedestal until the window closes
  wins, takes the demand and keeps the relic three days. Warriors are those on the barracks' muster roll; the
  rest are civilians, untouchable and untouching. The fallen go to the other side's prison for five to fifteen
  minutes and keep everything they carried; ransom and exchange free them sooner.
- A town's halls, prisons, barracks and houses cannot be broken by the enemy in a window, nor its chests opened
  or its fields fired. See `WAR.md`.

### Old forests and the traces of the Pioneers
- Old-growth and dead forest has windfalls: three to six logs of the local wood lying the same way, as a
  storm left them, among twigs and fallen leaves. Clearings bloom with meadow flowers, and berry bushes
  thicken along forest edges. TerraFirmaCraft already gives every stretch of forest an age; these follow it.
- Traces of the people who were here before: standing stones, cairns and lines of stones along vanished
  roads; the footings of houses with a cellar under a fallen floor, near water; grassed barrows over a
  stone cist on rises by rivers; dry-stone terraces stepping up hillsides; quarry pits with dressed blocks
  never carried away. Each is built of the stone and soil of the place it stands, and weathered.
- Cellar and barrow pots hold what survives in the ground: pottery, grain seed, bones, now and then a stone
  or copper tool. They keep clear of TFC Ruins. New worlds only; see `ideasformodpack/worldgen.md`.

### The Russian oven and bread
- A Russian oven (eight blocks of brick): lay logs on its hearth and light them; the brick stores the heat and,
  with the damper shut, keeps it for a day. The heat is told in words: fierce, hot, moderate, warm.
- Firmalife's leavened dough bakes into TerraFirmaCraft's bread on its hearth, plain dough into flatbread. The
  crust and the middle follow the heat: too hot burns the crust, too cool leaves it pale, too soon leaves it
  doughy. The loaf is poorly to finely made, which scales its food, its keeping and its Hearty effect.
- On the last of the heat the same hearth dries fruit. Take things out with a peel, or burn your hand.
  See `CUISINE.md`, "The Russian oven".

### Where a world starts
- Every new world starts within 1000 blocks of the spawn centre instead of 4000, so the first days are
  in the temperate band the pack is balanced for (5-6.5 C mean annual on the seeds measured) rather than
  anywhere from a frozen plateau to open sea. Existing worlds keep their spawn.
- New module `realism-worldgen`: TerraFirmaCraft's world preset with that one change, and tags naming the
  landmarks a traveller can take a bearing on (mesas, canyons, dunes, volcanoes, sea cliffs and more).
- tools/worldgen_survey.py: maps biomes, climate, rock and forest around spawn for three seeds without
  generating chunks; the agent gains /worldgen endpoints. Findings in `docs/worldgen/a0-survey.md`.

### Food and the body
- The same dish eaten again soon is enjoyed less: it gives back part of its saturation, its effects are
  shorter, and "You have had your fill of this" says so. It comes back after a few days away.
- Fruit and vegetables fill a store of fresh food that runs down over 20 days; sauerkraut keeps it, drying
  and cooking lose most of it. A winter with nothing fresh ends in scurvy: slower, weaker, wounds barely heal.
- A bowl from the cauldron is hot for a few hours. A hot one warms you through Cold Sweat; porridge and bread
  are Hearty (quicker digging and chopping), a broth with meat, fish or eggs is Restoring (faster healing).
- Starving no longer kills: it leaves a day of Exhaustion and half a heart. See `CUISINE.md`, "The body".
- Bowls ladled before this version count as cold, and a hot and a cold bowl do not stack.

### Illness as signs, and diagnosis
- A sick body shows signs, not the name of a disease: fever, gut cramps (the old "Dysentery" effect), an
  infected wound, and new spasms, rash, itch and sores.
- Four new diseases: lockjaw from a wound taken on dung or mud, typhoid from badly fouled water, scabies
  from a filthy bed or one a sick player slept in (at its worst the itch keeps you awake), anthrax from
  killing or handling sick farm animals.
- Right-click another player with an empty hand to examine them. A healer names a disease they know:
  three patients examined in a clinic or hospital, or enough reading on its topics, teach it.
  `/medicine cases` shows what you know. See `MEDICINE.md`.

### The mint
- A town can strike its own coin. A **coin die** (a bronze ingot and a hammer) placed in the core of a
  **mint** - a new building: an anvil, a forge, two chests and an archive cabinet in a closed room - by
  the town's head or treasurer is struck for the town. The first time, the head chooses the town's
  **arms**: one of twelve signs in one of sixteen colours, a pair no other town holds.
- The mint strikes **copper, silver and gold coins** as a work order from the core's new Orders page:
  one TFC ingot from the mint's chests makes ten coins in two calendar hours, eight ingots at a time.
  Gold needs a royal mint (two storeys over a cellar). Each coin carries the town's name and arms,
  drawn on the coin in the town's colour, and melts back into 10 mB in a crucible.
- The chronicle notes a town's arms and its first coin of each metal. A stolen die still strikes in
  another town's mint; nothing punishes that yet.

### Work orders
- Buildings can take work orders: a new recipe type `realism_institutions:institution_work`, run from
  the building's own chests by the calendar, pausing - never failing - while the building cannot work.
  The mint is the first building that uses them. `/institution orders [pos]` for operators.

### Roads
- Four tiers of road - trail, gravel road, cobbled road, paved road - make you (or the horse you ride)
  5 / 10 / 15 / 20% quicker, and a sprint along one costs that much less hunger. Tiers are block tags
  (`realism:roads/*`) holding TFC paths, aggregate, cobble, bricks and smooth stone with their slabs and
  stairs, and Macaw's paths and pavings.
- Trodden earth and plain gravel are streets only inside a town's border; beyond it a road has to be
  built of aggregate, cobble or paving. Numbers are in the `roads` section of
  `realism_polity-server.toml`.
- Stepping onto a road names it on the action bar now and then; a road block's tooltip and Jade say
  which road it makes.

### A pyrometer, and remedies that follow the seed
- A new instrument, the **pyrometer** (fire clay over a brass rod, a brass sheet and a brass rod).
  Right-click a firepit, grill, pot, crucible, blast furnace, firebox or charcoal forge with it, or
  hold hot work in the other hand, and it reads the fire to ±40 °C; the line goes straight into your
  notebook. A bloomery or a pit kiln keeps no scale to read, and says so.
- Yarrow poultice, meadowsweet chew and sphagnum dressing now draw their strength from the same
  seed-drawn law the field desk already reads for that plant, instead of a number fixed in code. An
  assay on the desk tells you in advance how good a dose will be in this world.

### The healer's hands
- A remedy can be used on somebody else: hold right-click on them. Treating yourself is always worse -
  one hand, and no view of the wound - and a splint cannot be put on yourself at all, which is the
  pack's one flat reason to go and find another player.
- A pair of hands has a count of procedures, per kind of work, shown only to their owner
  (`/medicine hands`). The first ten dressings hold worse and let more dirt in; after ten, practice
  stops paying, so there is nothing to grind. No level, no bar, no number out of a hundred.
- A dressing that does not hold does not fail outright: what is left of the bleeding, and what is
  left of the wound, is what got past it. A poor splint leaves part of the time that was on the bone.
- Fractures now say which bone. A fall breaks a leg, as before; a blunt blow can break the arm that
  took it, and a broken arm means no bow, no shield and slower digging. A hard blunt blow - a blast,
  a falling block, a maul - or a very long fall can leave a concussion, which comes in waves and
  passes off on its own. Rest in a good room shortens all of them.

### Apprenticeship
- A shared mechanism in the polity module, with medicine as its first user: a master takes an
  apprentice in a craft, and while the master is watching in the right building, the apprentice's
  work goes as well as the master's would and counts towards their apprenticeship. Twenty supervised
  procedures finish it, and nobody is taught the same craft twice.
- `/polity apprentice`, `/polity apprentice take <name> <craft>`, `/polity apprentice leave <craft>`.
  You can only take somebody whose name you know, standing with you.
- A master who has seen three apprentices through is named in the chronicle: the healer of a town if
  they hold a charter, a master healer if they hold none. The title is a line in the chronicle and
  nothing else.
- Modules declare their own crafts through `Crafts.declare`, so the machinery never enumerates them
  and the chronicle learns to name a craft it has never heard of.

### A lite client preset for weak machines
- A fifth graphics preset, **lite**, below low: for integrated graphics and 8 GB of memory. A 3 GB
  heap, 5 chunks, no mipmaps, minimal particles, no ambient occlusion, a 60 fps cap, one chunk
  builder thread. Physics Mod, Particle Rain, Sound Physics, Subtle Effects, the Fresh Animations
  layer (EMF/ETF), Caelum and AmbientSounds are left out of the game folder, as Distant Horizons and
  shaders already were. Terra Launcher recommends it by itself on such a machine; other launchers get
  it through `apply-preset lite` and the `lite` block in `jvm-args.txt`.
- A preset may carry its own JVM options: lite drops `-XX:+AlwaysPreTouch` and caps direct memory
  at 1 GB. Nothing changes on the server.
- Particle Core (client only) on every preset; lite and low ship a stricter config.

### Pet rats
- Naturalist's rats eat the pack's food: bread, cheese, grain, fruit and vegetables tame, tempt and
  breed them, and rotten food does not.
- Every rat has a favourite treat. Feeding it makes the rat spring into the air and grind its teeth;
  once found out, Jade shows it on your own rats.
- A clicker gives commands. Sit up, Spin and Up on the shoulder are learned by rewarding a rat with a
  treat within a few seconds of getting a trick right. A rat on your shoulder squeaks when something
  hostile is near and when food in your pack is about to spoil.
- Rat hammocks: tame rats sleep in one at night, up to four together.
- Maze feeders: bait one, build a maze and send your rat to find it. Each run it remembers is faster,
  and the time and record are reported.
- After a night slept through, a tame rat may bring a small present from `realism_compat:gameplay/rat_gift`.
- Litters of tame rats sometimes bring out a fancy colour - hooded, husky, Siamese, blue or champagne -
  which kittens then inherit. None of them spawns in the wild.
- A rat set to harvest into a chest now breaks the crop properly and replants from its drops, so the
  farm modules record the harvest instead of the crop resetting for free.
- A Companions chapter in the Field Guide.

### Institutions
- One core for every building. Right-click it and choose what the building is for: the survey becomes
  a checklist for that building, and a row can be clicked to outline in the world the blocks it
  counts. A core left without a purpose still works out for itself what a building is. Right-click a
  core in the air to list every building. The typed cores of the previous build are hidden and turn
  into the institution core with the same purpose when their world loads.
- Storeys: the scan counts floors, the stairs, ladders and hatches between them, cellars and attics.
  Building types can ask for them.
- Houses, from a hut to a manor. A player whose respawn point is a bed in a house is its resident; a
  house's comfort is for its residents, and the survey shows how many live there.
- The survey is a new screen: tabs for the room, its equipment, its collection, its grades and what it
  does; a tick or a cross beside every rule; and beside every facility the blocks that count for it,
  listed on hover. `/institution survey [pos]` opens it without reaching the core.
- Institution cores and the printing press drop when broken with a pickaxe. Before, no tool counted
  and breaking one destroyed it.
- Recognised buildings now act on the world. A greenhouse keeps its planted rooms above 5 °C, and
  above 12 °C and more humid once it is heated; barns, granaries, root cellars and ice houses slow the
  decay of food in their stores; barns and stables keep TFC animals tame; inns, clinics and hospitals
  shorten bleeding and fractures while you rest in them; universities and laboratories teach flags
  that scripts can check with `Institutions.hasFlag`.
- Six new building types: barn, granary, root cellar, ice house, stable and inn.
- The space rules `max_sky` and `min_depth`, for buildings that must be roofed or underground.
- `/institution effects [pos]`, effect lines in the survey, and an effects tooltip on the core in Jade.
- A bed is counted once, by its head: a survey used to count both halves, so an infirmary, an inn or
  a house needed only half the beds it asked for.
- A root cellar now holds its air between 2 and 8 °C and adds humidity; its vaulted tier holds a
  narrower 3…6 °C. An ice house holds −4…1 °C. A crock counts as the cellar's storage, so a cellar can
  be built out of crocks.

### People
- A new module, Polity. On first join you choose a name and something that marks you out; until you
  do, nothing in the world can hurt you and you cannot touch it.
- Strangers see "Stranger (mark)" in chat and the tab list, and nothing over your head. Tell somebody
  your name by crouching and right-clicking them with an empty hand, or say it aloud to everyone within
  8 blocks with a new key (unbound by default) or `/introduce`. A learned name is not forgotten.
- Operators see account names beside everything, put a name right with `/polity name set`, and make a
  player choose again with `/polity name reset`.

### Towns
- A **town hall** is a building type like any other: 36 square metres, two tables, an archive shelf
  and four reading seats, in three grades - moot hall, council hall, great hall.
- A **town seal** of copper and wood. Blank, pressed into a recognised hall's core, it asks what the
  town is to be called and is struck with that name; struck, it gives a town back a hall it lost.
- **Citizens.** A charter from the head makes you admitted; a recognised house inside the border makes
  you a citizen. One charter at a time; three days between laying one down and taking another;
  fourteen days after an exile before that town will have you again.
- **A border** round the hall: 48, 64 or 80 blocks by its grade, sixteen more for every citizen and
  eight for every building inside it, never past 256. Where two would cross, each stops at half the
  distance between the halls. A town that loses its hall keeps the border it had.
- Crouch and right-click a hall's core with an empty hand to read the town: its head, its grade, where
  its border came from, its citizens, and - to the head - who is asking to be let in.
- Every client is told every border, and map sheets draw them in each town's own ink.
- `/polity town list|info`, `/polity leave`, and for operators `town rename|head|dissolve` and
  `citizen grant|revoke`.
- Breaking a recognised core now tells the other modules the building is lost, and a core's sealed item
  can be read and replaced without measuring the building again.

### The chronicle and the archive
- The world keeps a **chronicle**: towns founded, charters granted, laid down and revoked, exiles,
  halls lost and raised again, a town's first building of a kind, and everybody who arrives or takes a
  new name. Any module can write into it.
- On joining you are told what happened while you were away - your town, any town founded or ended, and
  anything that named you. A newcomer gets the last lines of the world instead.
- The chronicle is read at a hall, from a library's catalogue, or with `/polity chronicle`.
- Every town keeps an **archive**: charters of founding and citizenship, exiles, charters laid down and
  decrees. A charter costs the head a sheet of paper and is handed to the citizen; a copy from the
  archive costs a sheet too.
- A paper says what the archive says today, so a revoked charter reads as revoked in anyone's hands.
- `/polity decree "<title>" <text>` for a head, `/polity document revoke <id>` for an operator.

### The board and the post
- Every town hall has a **board**: "I need twenty bronze ingots, I pay five copper". Posting a notice
  puts the payment into the board's keeping, so the pay is a fact and not a promise; whoever brings
  what is asked takes the payment there and then, and the goods wait at the hall for the poster.
- A notice is written with your hands: what you are paying with in the main hand, one of what you need
  in the other, and the page only asks how many. Three notices each, twenty-four to a board, and a
  notice stands fourteen days before it comes down with its payment still on it.
- **Letters** between players, written on a sheet of your own paper to somebody whose name you know.
  A letter is signed, so one that arrives teaches its reader the writer's name - the post spreads
  acquaintance the same one-way way that meeting does.
- On joining you are told what is waiting: letters, and any board holding something of yours. The line
  opens the box when it is clicked, as does `/polity mail`.
- A box holds thirty-two letters; a new one drops the oldest you have already read, and a box full of
  unread letters takes no more, so nobody can bury somebody else's post.

### The treasury and its upkeep
- Every hall keeps a **treasury**: 27, 54 or 81 cells by the hall's grade, filled and drawn on by
  anybody within reach, merged into matching stacks the way a chest is. Only the head or the
  **treasurer** - an office granted by paper, like a charter - may withdraw or spend it. Every
  movement is written to a ledger, ten lines to a page, read by anybody standing at the hall.
- Every building inside a town's border, except its houses and its hall, costs something a week -
  paper, candles, fuel, cloth or lumber, by what kind of building it is - drawn from the treasury
  without anybody asking. A building a day past due **stands idle**: nothing can reach it, its
  effects stop, it teaches nothing, and it stops counting towards the border, until the treasury
  can pay it again.
- A building outside every town's border pays nothing and never stands idle - a frontier building is
  cheap to keep, and grows nobody's border for it.
- The head or treasurer can post a **treasury order** on the board, paid for out of the treasury and
  signed with the town's own name; what is brought for it goes straight into the treasury.
- Struck out, a town's treasury goes to its head, or falls at the hall if there is nobody to hand it
  to.
- A **Treasury** tab on the town screen, next to the board, chronicle and archive.
  `/polity treasury [town]`, `/polity treasury ledger [town] [page]`, and for operators
  `/polity town treasurer <town> <player|none>`, `/polity upkeep bill <town>`,
  `/polity treasury open <town>` and `/polity clock add <hours>`.

### Measurement, and the notebook that keeps it
- Some laws of the world are now drawn from its **seed**: how strong a medicinal plant is, how much
  metal an ore carries. The shape of the law is fixed, the value is this world's, and no wiki can
  answer it - the only way to know is to measure it here. Nothing is saved: a value follows from the
  seed and the law's name, so it cannot drift. `/research constants` dumps them to an operator, and
  to nobody else.
- Measuring gives an **interval**, not a number. How narrow it is depends on the building the
  instrument stands in; two readings of one thing combine so that four halve the interval, and two
  readings only contradict each other past what both instruments could be wrong by.
- The **field desk** assays: hold up a piece of ore, or crouch with a specimen, and it reads out
  "61 ± 15 %" and uses the sample up. A narrower answer costs more samples, as it always has.
- The **field notebook** (leather and three sheets of paper) is written by the instrument, not by
  you: every reading goes in with its place, day and instrument. Right-click to read the last lines.
  The book is the key to the record, so it can be dropped, taken off a body, traded or inherited -
  and crouching with a blank notebook in the other hand, in a building that can copy, copies it out
  for a sheet of paper.
- A furnace's temperature is named as a quantity but is not drawn from the seed: it is a fact about
  the fire in front of you, and the pyrometer above is what reads it.

### The byre reports
- A recognised byre counts its stock once a day: how many have nothing to drink, nothing to eat,
  have gone thin, are not right, and whether they are packed too tight to lie down.
- You are told what it found when you next log in - about a byre you logged out beside, or one in
  the town whose charter you hold. At most three byres at once, worst first; thirst and hunger come
  before a thin animal, because they are today's problem.
- Nothing about the model changed: neglect is still a setback and never a loss. Animals go thin,
  stop milking and stop breeding, and take it all back when they are fed. This is only the half that
  was missing - finding out.

### The weeks of the year
- Five windows taken from the TerraFirmaCraft calendar - the sowing, the haymaking, the harvest, the
  rut and the freeze. Each is written into the chronicle once a year when it comes round, and each is
  a line you are greeted with while it is open.
- They change nothing about what the world allows. A field is sown when you sow it; the calendar only
  says out loud what week it is.

### Kitchen
- A new module, Cuisine. Stand a tripod on a firepit, hang a copper cauldron from it, pour in water or milk and
  put food in: a pottage or a porridge is built from what went in, named for it, and graded from poorly to
  finely made.
- A ladle tastes the pot - the fire, how done, how it tastes - and stirs it while held. The hook sets the heat.
- Quality multiplies a portion's nutrition and slows its decay; a pot makes up to two portions per item.
- Borscht, shchi, ukha, kulesh and milk porridge are recognised from what is in the pot, and some ingredients
  pair.
- Undercooked meat, fish, eggs and a few roots and beans make you ill.
- Crouch and right-click a full cauldron, or use `/cuisine inside <pos>`, to see what is in it.
- TerraFirmaCraft's pot soup and Farmer's Delight's cooking pot are unchanged.
- Varieties: apples, strawberries, gooseberries and cabbage come as Antonovka or White Naliv, Woodland or Musk,
  Slava or Amager - sixteen in all. A wild plant grows the variety of its place; cabbage seed carries its variety
  into a garden. A variety tastes of itself in the cauldron, feeds a little more or less, and keeps longer or
  shorter. `/cuisine varieties <pos>` shows what grows where.
- Gooseberries go in the cauldron.
- Two new blocks keep food: a **crock** sours cabbage or soaks fruit under a weight, and a **drying
  line** strung between posts dries fruit or cures salted meat and fish. Both go by the calendar and
  the place they stand in - a crock in a warm house sours in days and turns oversour by midsummer in
  the same spot; moved to a cellar it keeps until spring. A crock or line asleep in an unloaded chunk
  catches up the weather it missed rather than the moment it wakes. A ladle or a crouched look gives
  words, not numbers; `/cuisine preserve <pos>` gives an operator the numbers for check scripts.
- Salted, pickled and smoked food now tastes of it in the cauldron, the same way a variety does - not
  only what a crock or line just made, but TFC's own salting, brining, pickling and smoking. Salted
  meat or fish already brings its own salt to the pot, so a dish built with it and more salt besides
  comes out oversalted - nothing in the pack removes the `tfc:salted` trait, so leave the extra salt
  out rather than trying to soak it away.
- A portion taken from a crock before its technique is ready loses the keeping trait it would have
  been marked with, the way TFC's own vessels strip a trait opened too soon; ready and oversour
  portions keep it.

### Farming and livestock
- TerraFirmaCraft's cows, goats, yaks, sheep, alpacas, musk oxen and pigs now have a body kept on the
  animal: weight, condition, milk in the udder, fleece, pregnancy and pedigree. Condition follows what
  they graze and are fed, the weather, shelter and crowding.
- A milking gives what is in the udder and a shearing what fleece has grown, so a thin cow gives less.
  Thin, sick or closely related animals often fail to get in calf; calves inherit from both parents and
  their inbreeding is tracked.
- Crops a player plants grow on accumulated warmth instead of TFC's timer, draw on their farmland's
  nutrients and water, can be killed by frost and disease, and drop what their season earned. A
  harvested field counts as one season of its rotation.
- Jade shows an animal's breed, condition, milk, pregnancy and inbreeding, and a crop's development,
  what holds it back and its expected yield. Operators get `/husbandry inspect|debug` and
  `/agriculture adopt`.
- Feed troughs, hay racks, water troughs and bedding. Animals eat and drink from them on their own; a
  trough holds a ration, and bedding soils and has to be mucked out.
- Dung falls where the animals are: onto the pasture, or into the bedding of a barn. A manure heap
  composts it from how big, wet, aired and warm it is. A well-kept heap heats past 55 °C and becomes
  compost that is safe to spread, while a sodden, unturned one stays cold and loses its nitrogen.
- A barn's troughs, bedding and ventilation openings now count toward how well it houses its animals.
- Pests in a field fed twice on every growth step; they feed once now.
- Livestock grazing a scarce species no longer eat more of it than the pasture has.

### Health and water
- Anything that breaks the skin carries dirt in: a little on a blade, a lot on teeth and claws, more
  on a dung heap. The wound stays open to dirt for five minutes unless it is dressed.
- Whether it festers is decided by how much dirt got in, how soon it was cleaned, and how well fed
  and rested the body is. Nothing is left to chance. A sphagnum dressing draws dirt out, and yarrow
  cleans a little; a bandage only covers the wound.
- New conditions: open wound, infected wound (heals slowly, weakens attacks), fever (slows, burns
  food, sweats water away) and dysentery (weakens, burns food and drains TerraFirmaCraft thirst fast).
  Each ends when the body wins, shows as a bar under the injuries, and has its own icon; bleeding and
  fracture now have icons too, instead of the missing-texture square.
- Water can be foul. Dung on the ground washes into nearby ponds, more after rain, and dies off within
  days once the animals leave. A stream carries less than a still pond. A well dug down through the
  ground is filtered by it. Murky or bitter water says so; water carrying disease looks and tastes
  like any other.
- A jug, bottle, bucket or water flask keeps what was in the water it was filled from. A pot held at
  the boil on a firepit kills what lives in its water, but leaves anything dissolved in it.
- Rotten food can give you dysentery. When it starts, the message says what probably caused it: the
  water you drank at a place, water you carried, or spoiled food.
- Meadowsweet also eases a fever.

### Research
- Chat no longer names a species you have only seen, sampled or tested. It shows the kind of thing
  ("Unknown fungus") until the species is identified. This covers first sightings, specimens and
  answered investigations.
- Confirming an investigation on site no longer identifies a species without a laboratory.

### Forestry
- Axe wear follows the wood's hardness. Before, every swing cost exactly one point of durability, so
  ebony dulled an axe no faster than pine.
- Timber from a felled tree is green and seasons over the following months. Light softwoods like
  spruce are ready in about half a year of game time, dense hardwoods like oak take most of a year.
  The tooltip shows a log's moisture and how many days it has left.
- Green wood burns cooler, shorter and smokier in every TerraFirmaCraft fire (firepits, forges, blast
  furnaces, fireboxes, ovens), and TFC's fuel tooltip shows the lower numbers. A charcoal pit of green
  logs yields less charcoal, in TFC's pit and in TFC Woodworking's.
- Logs that were not freshly felled - from a building taken apart, from before this update, or from
  another mod - count as seasoned.

- TreeChop is switched off in its config. The notch is now the only way a tree comes down; before,

- Physics Mod (client): blocks break into pieces, mobs fall as ragdolls, dropped items tumble. Its

- `assemble_pack.py --private` lays jars from the untracked `pack/private/` over the client pack, for

- MODLIST.md lists every audited mod again: seven curated sections were missing from the generator's
